statement: Prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers.
heath_proof: Let A, B, C be the assigned prime numbers; I say that there are more prime numbers than A, B, C. For let the least number measured by A, B, C be taken, and let it be DE; let the unit DF be added to DE. Then EF is either prime or not. First, let it be prime; then the prime numbers A, B, C, EF have been found which are more than A, B, C. Next, let EF not be prime; therefore it is measured by some prime number. [VII. 31] Let it be measured by the prime number G. I say that G is not the same with any of the numbers A, B, C. For, if possible, let it be so. Now A, B, C measure DE; therefore G also will measure DE. But it also measures EF. Therefore G, being a number, will measure the remainder, the unit DF: which is absurd. Therefore G is not the same with any one of the numbers A, B, C. And by hypothesis it is prime. Therefore the prime numbers A, B, C, G have been found which are more than the assigned multitude of A, B, C.
ai_proof_text:
9.20
**Statement:** Prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C be the assigned prime numbers (the argument is the same for any assigned multitude, three being taken as representative). I say that there are more prime numbers than A, B, C.

**Step 2.** Take the least number DE which A, B, C measure [7.36], so that each of A, B, C measures DE; and to DE add the unit DF, so that EF is a number made up of DE together with the unit DF. (Any number measured by A, B, C, for instance their product, would serve here; the least such number is chosen because 7.36 supplies it in a single step.)

**Step 3.** EF either is prime or is measured by some prime number [7.32]. (7.32 is invoked rather than 7.31 because it yields exactly the alternative required, without first establishing that EF is composite.)

**Step 4.** First, let EF be prime. Then EF is not the same as any of A, B, C. For each of A, B, C measures DE, and a number which measures another is the less of the two, a part of it, or else equal to it [D7.3]; hence none of A, B, C is greater than DE. But EF is greater than DE, since DE is a part of EF [CN5]. Therefore EF is greater than each of A, B, C, and so is a prime number different from all of them. Thus the prime numbers A, B, C, EF have been found, more in multitude than the assigned A, B, C.

**Step 5.** Next, let EF not be prime. Then, by Step 3, EF is measured by some prime number G. I say that G is not the same as any of A, B, C.

**Step 6.** For, if possible, let G be the same as one of A, B, C. Since each of A, B, C measures DE (Step 2), G measures DE. But G also measures EF. Now EF is made up of parts each equal to G, and DE, which is a part of EF, is likewise made up of parts each equal to G; therefore the remainder DF, which is what is left of EF when DE is taken away, is also made up of parts each equal to G. That is, G measures DF.

**Step 7.** But DF is a unit. Since G measures DF, DF is not less than G [D7.3]. Yet G, being a number, is a multitude composed of units [D7.2], and so is greater than a single unit, the unit being a part of it [CN5]; that is, DF is less than G. Thus DF would be at once not less than G and less than G, which is absurd. Therefore G is not the same as any of A, B, C.

**Step 8.** And G is prime (Step 5). Therefore the prime numbers A, B, C, G have been found, more in multitude than the assigned A, B, C.

**Step 9.** Hence in either case a prime number has been found which is different from every one of A, B, C. Since the assigned multitude A, B, C was arbitrary, prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers. Q.E.D.
